question.text: Rebalancing VIA INFLOWS is tax-efficient because:

answer.text: Uses new cash to buy underweight positions, avoiding sales and capital gains tax

explanation.text: The Logic: A portfolio drifts away from its target allocation as some sleeves outperform others. Traditional rebalancing brings the portfolio back by trimming the overweight (appreciated) sleeve and buying the underweight one — but the sale of appreciated assets crystallises capital gains and triggers tax. "Rebalancing via inflows" routes new cash (fresh contributions, dividends, coupon income) preferentially into the underweight sleeves until the target weights are restored. Because no appreciated asset is sold, there is no realised gain and no associated capital-gains tax event, which is what makes the technique tax-efficient. The Trap: "No tax" is too absolute — the technique avoids realised capital gains on rebalancing trades, but ongoing income (interest, dividends, distributions) is still taxable. "No fees" is also wrong: inflow rebalancing still incurs purchase costs/charges, just like any allocation. The claim that SEBI forbids it is incorrect; using fresh cash to true up allocations is a standard, allowed practice. Note: The specific claim that inflow-based rebalancing avoids sales and capital-gains tax is not directly stated on the cited NISM Series XXI-B Portfolio Managers workbook pages checked (pp.185-186, 311, 396-397), although those pages do support the related point that selling appreciated assets during rebalancing creates tax liabilities. The framing above reflects general industry/practitioner knowledge of tax-efficient rebalancing rather than the cited workbook chapter.
